beginner: There are three easy ways. The simplest is to sow seed right in the garden, a quarter to a half inch deep, then thin the seedlings to about one per inch. Or start seeds indoors about four weeks before planting out for an earlier harvest, then set the little plants an inch apart. The tidiest way is to multisow: drop a small pinch of about six to ten seeds into each cell, let them grow as a little clump, and plant the whole clump out without splitting it, about four to six inches from the next one. Because you eat scallions in bunches anyway, there is nothing to thin, and you just pull the biggest few from each clump and let the rest keep growing. Bunching kinds can also be split from an existing clump.
seasoned: Three easy routes. Direct-sow seed in a two-inch-wide band, a quarter to a half inch deep, in rows 12 to 18 inches apart, then thin to about one plant per inch (UMN); this is the simplest method and suits succession sowing. Or start seed indoors about four weeks before set-out for an earlier first cutting, transplanting seedlings an inch apart. The tidiest indoor route is to multisow: sow a pinch of about six to ten seeds per cell, grow the cluster on undivided, and set the whole clump out without separating it, spacing clumps four to six inches apart; scallions are pulled as a bunch, so there is no thinning, and you take the biggest from each clump first and let the rest size up (RHS). Bunching types can also be multiplied by dividing established clumps.

beginner: There are two kinds. Bunching onions like Evergreen Hardy White or Tokyo Long White never make a bulb, grow back after cutting, and many survive winter, so they are great for a patch you keep cutting. Regular onions like White Lisbon, sown close together and pulled young, give a fast scallion but you pull the whole plant once. Either works for the kitchen.
seasoned: Choose between two habits. True bunching types (Allium fistulosum) such as Evergreen Hardy White, Tokyo Long White, Beltsville Bunching, and Parade never form a bulb and many are perennial and very cold hardy, ideal for cut-and-come-again clumps. Regular bulb onions sown thickly and pulled young, such as White Lisbon, give a quick straight scallion but are pulled once, not divided. Clemson names Beltsville Bunching and Evergreen Bunching among types bred specifically for green-onion use.

beginner: Scallions are good neighbors for carrots, beets, lettuce, and cabbage-family plants, mostly because their strong smell is thought to keep some pests away, and they are small enough to slip between other crops. The main thing to avoid is planting them next to beans or peas, since onions can slow those down. These are helpful traditions, not sure things, so do not worry if your garden does a little differently.
seasoned: Scallions earn their companion reputation mostly through their allium scent, traditionally credited with deterring aphids and the carrot rust fly, so they pair well with carrots, beets, lettuce, and brassicas, and tuck neatly between slower crops. The one firm caution is the legume conflict: alliums are widely held to inhibit beans and peas, so keep scallions away from them. Most of these claims are traditional rather than trial-proven; treat them as low-risk suggestions, not guarantees.

beginner: Scallions and carrots are a classic garden pair. Their strong smell is said to help hide carrots from the carrot rust fly, and the two plants do not crowd each other's roots.
seasoned: Carrots and scallions are the textbook reciprocal pairing. Your scallions' sulfur scent helps mask the carrots from the carrot rust fly, and in return carrots interplanted with scallions tend to carry less scallion thrips damage, so each crop disrupts the other's main pest. Intercropping trials have measured real reductions in carrot fly where the two grow together. Plant in alternating rows with enough scallion density for the scent-masking to register, and note the strongest results come from small mixed plantings rather than large solid blocks.

beginner: Beets and scallions grow well side by side. They like the same cool weather and stay out of each other's way.
seasoned: Beets and scallions share a bed comfortably. The onion's pungency helps deter pests that bother beets, and because scallions shank shallowly with sparse upright foliage while beets put their energy into a single root, the two do not crowd each other above or below ground. This is mostly a good-neighbor, efficient-space pairing with a modest pest-repel bonus.

beginner: Fast little lettuce plants fit nicely in the gaps between scallions and like the same cool season, so you get two crops from one spot.
seasoned: Lettuce and scallions interplant efficiently. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick while scallions send a narrow shank down with little leafy spread, so they occupy different space and the lettuce fills in between scallion rows. The scallion scent offers a little aphid deterrence over the lettuce as a bonus. Treat it as a space-and-timing pairing first, mild pest help second.

beginner: Cabbage and broccoli like the same cool weather as scallions, and the strong scallion smell is thought to bother some of their pests.
seasoned: Scallions are a well-supported brassica companion. Their sulfur scent helps mask the cabbage family and deter its signature pests, cabbage loopers, worms, and root maggots, and extension trial work including scallion in a mix with broccoli showed reduced caterpillar damage. Alliums are shallow and undemanding, so they tuck between brassicas without competing for the heavy feeding those crops want.

beginner: Instead of planting all your scallions at once, sow a short row every couple of weeks. That way they are ready a few at a time over many weeks. seasoned: Scallions are a natural succession crop: sow a short row every two to three weeks through the cool season rather than one big planting, so they mature in sequence and none over-mature. The number of sowings is set by the length of your cool window, not a fixed cap.

seasoned: In the cold-winter North, scallions are an easy cool-season crop you can grow from spring right through fall. They tolerate the northern summer better than most cool-season crops, so there is no real summer gap; the season simply closes when the ground freezes. Very cold-hardy bunching types can even overwinter under mulch for an extra-early spring cutting.

beginner: A spring onion, also called a scallion or green onion, is a young onion you eat whole: the long white base and the green tops. You harvest it before it makes a round bulb, so it grows fast and is easy. Some kinds (called bunching onions) never make a bulb at all, and you can also just sow regular onions close together and pull them young as scallions. Plant the seeds shallow, thin the seedlings to about an inch apart, keep the soil damp, and they are usually ready in about 50 to 70 days, when the green tops are 6 to 8 inches tall. They handle cold well, so plant a short row every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, and nearly year-round where winters are mild.
seasoned: Spring onion, or scallion, is a fast cool-season allium grown for its slender white shank and green tops rather than a mature bulb. It is harvested young, before bulbing, so the day-length trigger that governs bulb onions is irrelevant here: you pull the plant while it is still a straight stem. Two routes give the same kitchen result, true bunching types (Allium fistulosum) that never form a bulb, or regular bulb onions (Allium cepa) sown thickly and pulled at the green stage. Sow seed shallowly, thin to about an inch, keep the soil evenly moist, and harvest in roughly 50 to 70 days when the tops stand 6 to 8 inches. Because the crop is quick and very cold hardy, sow a short row every two to three weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, year-round in mild regions.

beginner: Your scallions are ready when the green tops are about 6 to 8 inches tall and the white bottom is roughly as thick as a pencil. Do not wait for a round bulb to form, pull them while the base is still straight. Lift the whole plant, or with bunching types snip the tops about an inch above the soil and let them grow back. Smaller ones taste milder, bigger ones are a little stronger.
seasoned: Pull scallions once the green tops reach about 6 to 8 inches and the white shank is roughly pencil thick. There is no need to wait for a bulb: harvest at the straight-stem stage, before the base swells. Lift the whole plant, or cut bunching types about an inch above the crown and let them regrow. Younger is milder, so harvest on the small side for salads and a bit larger for cooking.
